summary:
South Kalimantan is a province of Indonesia, and a visitor here stands under the national framework that governs the country as a whole. The source inventory records no South Kalimantan-specific provision on gender identity, documents, facilities or enforcement: no provincial criminalisation of trans people, no provincial marker rule of its own, and no documented local divergence from the national position.

Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The 2023 penal code was passed by the House of Representatives on 6 December 2022, signed by President Joko Widodo, and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment. It sets a penalty of up to one year's imprisonment for sexual activity outside marriage where a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, but because Indonesia does not recognise same-sex marriage, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls within the outside-marriage restriction. International criticism, including from the United Nations, is recorded for its failure to accommodate protections and rights for LGBT individuals and domestic partnerships.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids. On 22 June 2025, Indonesian police raided a privately rented villa in the Puncak area near Bogor after public reports of a "gay party" and arrested 75 people, 74 men and one woman. Amnesty International's Deputy Director Wirya Adiwena described the operation as a blatant violation of human rights and privacy and stated that the gathering violated no law.

There is a directly documented death of a trans traveler in Indonesian custody. Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla, a Harvard student and trans activist from Peru, was arrested at an Indonesian airport on drug charges while on honeymoon in Bali in 2022. During a WhatsApp call, his mother in Lima was told that authorities demanded up to US$100,000 for his release. He died in custody; his mother alleges that police beat him, while Indonesian police have denied that violence was used.

Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

Gender identity itself is not criminalised under national law, there is no X-marker option on Indonesian identity documents, and same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. Since June 2021 the Ministry of Home Affairs has run outreach issuing transgender Indonesians identification papers, with only male and female sex descriptors recognised and the birth-gender descriptor printed unless a court order was already obtained; electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces.

Transgender identity, known as waria, has long been part of Indonesian culture, which shapes everyday visibility in public life. Cultural presence has not translated into legal protection: documented repressive incidents include raids on transgender women by the Jakarta Social Agency and the January 2021 flogging of two men in Aceh province.

The turbulence recorded nationally since 2025 reaches transgender people directly, from the June 2025 Puncak villa raid and the arrest of 75 people, to the October 2025 presidential decree placing LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy, to reporting from August 2026 on waves of vigilante attacks against transgender women.

The death of Rodrigo Ventocilla Ventosilla in custody in 2022 establishes that a trans foreign national has died in Indonesian detention under disputed circumstances, with allegations of police beating and a denial of violence from Indonesian police.
localsOnly:
Indonesian citizens who are transgender have been able to obtain identification papers through Ministry of Home Affairs outreach running since June 2021. Only male and female sex descriptors are recognised, and the descriptor assigned at birth is printed on the card unless a court order was obtained beforehand; electronic ID cards were issued to transgender people in nine provinces.

The 2023 penal code, in force from 2 January 2026, exposes residents to up to one year's imprisonment for sexual activity outside marriage where an immediate family member complains, and the broader extra-marital provision carries up to two years. Same-sex couples have no route around this through marriage, which is not legally recognised.

There is no national anti-discrimination protection covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no legal recognition of a sex marker outside male or female. Transgender people face administrative raids on their own social spaces, as documented in the Jakarta Social Agency operations on transgender women.
